The story presents a variety of perspectives, most notably that of the thirteen-year-old narrator, who begins the trip feeling resentful, guarded, and somewhat unlikable in her "questions that were really accusations" toward her dying father. The writer convincingly and empathetically portrays her adolescent self-centeredness and feelings of rejection—such as viewing her father's friends as people who took him away from her—not as malice, but as the understandable confusion of a child trying to make sense of her parents' separation. Furthermore, the story subtly conveys the perspectives of the mother (whose hurt is evident in the "silences" and her loaded tone), the father (who patiently makes space for his daughter's difficult emotions while facing his own mortality), his supportive circle of friends, and Julian, a teenager who offers a contrasting, well-adjusted perspective on having gay parents.
